L1588: 6.4 Performance comparison of defense approaches against our 513

L1598: Approach: We evaluate the eﬀectiveness of our proposed ASTT approach on three 518
L1599: defense approaches following the previous research [12]. For poisoning vulnerabilities in 519
L1600:

L1604:

L1606:

L1608: from clean examples. If the defender is certain that poisoned code segments can be 524
L1609:

L1611:

L1701: 7.1 The characteristics of unsuccessful attacks 565
L1702: As shown in Yang et al.’s work [13], their triggers inevitably sacriﬁced some attack 566
L1703: 
L1704: eﬀectiveness. The intuition is that the poisoned examples are harder to distinguish 567
L1705: 
L1706: from benign examples. Based on the results of RQ1, similar issues exist in our designed 568
L1707: 
L1708: trigger. Any code segment having the speciﬁc node sequence will be injected with 569
L1709: 
L1710: malicious code segments in the output code segment. In the actual reasoning phase,570
L1711: some code segments will inevitably be injected with malicious code segments by mis-571
L1712: 
L1713: take. If there are too many code segments injected with malicious code segments, it 572
L1714: 
L1715: will lead to the failure of backdoor attacks. The key to solving this issue is to select a 573
L1716: 
L1717: node sequence with extremely high diﬀerentiation as the trigger. This requires com-574
L1718: 
L1719: prehensively considering the training dataset’s size, the node sequence length, and the 575
L1720: 
L1721: attack success rate.576
L1722: 7.2 Complexity and overhead analysis of our proposed 577
L1723: 
L1724: approach 578
L1725: 
L1726: Deep learning-based model training includes multiple stages such as data collection,579
L1727: 
L1728: model training, model validation, and model testing. Poisoning attacks occur in the 580
L1729: 
L1730: data collection phase. The scenario we consider is that a malicious insider poisons the 581
L1731: 
L1732: training data to implant a backdoor. So, we mainly considered the complexity and 582
L1733: 
L1734: overhead analysis of our proposed approach during the data collection phase.583
L1735: First, we analyze the time complexity of diﬀerent data processing algorithms. When 584
L1736: 
L1737: we build a deep learning model with raw data, we only need to adjust the input 585
L1738: 
L1739: format according to the requirements of the deep learning model. The algorithmic time 586
L1740: 
L1741: complexity of this data preprocessing process is O(1). When we perform a poisoning 587
L1742: 
L1743: attack on the training dataset based on dead code insertion, as the size (n) of the 588
L1744: training dataset increases, then the preprocessing time also increases linearly, so the 589
L1745: 
L1746: time complexity of this algorithm is O(n). For our proposed approach ASTT, the K−590
L1747: 
L1748: means algorithm is our core algorithm for poisoning attacks, and the time complexity 591
L1749: 
L1750: of this K−means algorithm determines the time complexity of ASTT. The time 592
L1751: 
L1752: complexity of the K−means algorithm mainly depends on the size of the data set (n),593
L1753: the number of clustering centers (k), and the number of iterations (t). In general, the 594
L1754: 
L1755: time complexity of the K−means algorithm can be approximated as O(n×k×t×d),595
L1756: 
L1757: where d is the dimension of the data points.596
L1758: 
L1759: Second, we empirically investigate the time overhead of diﬀerent data processing 597
L1760: 
L1761: algorithms on three downstream tasks using the system environment as described in 598

L1764: has the highest time complexity, followed by the dead code-based poisoning attack 600
L1765:
